Study method details: Case report of 3 adults who presented to an emergency department 1.5 h after eating a foraged plant believed to be Allium tricoccum; serum digoxin measured on arrival and repeated approximately 12 h later. Plant material (roots, stem, leaves, flowers) was later ground under liquid nitrogen, extracted in methanol, and analysed by high-performance liquid chromatography (Thermo Scientific Ultimate 3000) with high-resolution mass spectrometry (Thermo Scientific Q Exactive Orbitrap) against reference standards of convallatoxin, cyclopamine and veratridine.
Physiologically realistic concentration?: not reported in the information source

Notes: This PDF provides NO convallatoxin-attributable interference measurement: qualitative HPLC-HRMS analysis of the plant specimen was negative for convallatoxin (positive for cyclopamine), and the authors conclude "it seems extremely unlikely that this plant was lily of the valley" and that "the detectable digoxin concentrations in all 3 patients were likely false positives" attributable to Veratrum steroidal alkaloids. All three direction columns and the significance cell therefore carry the missing literal - assigning a direction to convallatoxin here would be inference beyond the page. The paper states only narratively that "C majalis causes a detectable digoxin concentration via its cardiac steroid compound (convallatoxin) that is similar to digoxin", with no quantitative data. Repeat digoxin: 1.3 ng·mL-1 (repeat, approximately 12.5 h from time of ingestion, after 20 vials (800 mg) of digoxin-specific antibody fragments). Presentation: lowest blood pressure 81/53 mm Hg, lowest heart rate 44 beats·min-1, initial potassium 3.6 mEq·L-1. Digoxin assay and analyzer are not named anywhere in the PDF. Internal discrepancy in this PDF, recorded and not reconciled: the Abstract (p 340) and Case Report (p 341) print this patient's blood pressure as 81/43 mm Hg while Table 1 (p 342) prints 81/53 mm Hg.
